Binary Object Format

1. What is the Binary Object Format?
  • Ignite serializes all data entries into a compact binary object format before storing them;
  • This is Ignite's internal serialization format — it is not Java serialization;
  • Binary objects are stored in off-heap memory (outside the JVM heap);
2. Why use Binary Objects?
  • Field-level access without deserialization — you can read individual fields from a binary object without deserializing the entire object; this is significantly faster for server-side operations;
  • No class on the server classpath — server nodes do not need the Java class definitions; only the binary format matters;
  • Schema evolution — you can add or remove fields from objects of the same type; different clients with different class versions can coexist;
  • Cross-platform — binary objects enable interoperability between Java, .NET, C++, and other clients;
  • Dynamic type creation — you can construct objects by type name without having class definitions;
3. Working with Binary Objects
  • Access the binary view of a cache using withKeepBinary(): 
    IgniteCache<Integer, BinaryObject> binaryCache =
    ignite.cache("myCache").withKeepBinary();

BinaryObject binaryObj = binaryCache.get(1);

// Read individual fields without full deserialization
String name = binaryObj.field("name");
int age = binaryObj.field("age");
  • Build a binary object dynamically: 
    BinaryObject person = ignite.binary().builder("Person")
    .setField("name", "Alice")
    .setField("age", 30)
    .setField("city", "NYC")
    .build();

binaryCache.put(1, person);
4. Modifying Binary Objects
  • Binary objects are immutable; to modify one, create a new builder from the existing object: 
    BinaryObject updated = binaryObj.toBuilder()
    .setField("age", 31)
    .removeField("city")
    .build();

binaryCache.put(1, updated);
5. When to use Binary Objects
  • When server nodes should not have application classes on the classpath;
  • When you need to access a single field without deserializing the entire object (e.g., in CacheEntryProcessor);
  • When building generic tooling or admin UIs that work with any data type;
  • When you need cross-platform access (.NET reading data written by Java);
